(u)efi is the new flavor of BIOS. Where BIOS (the black screen with settings you could call up when your computer starts) was baked on a chip, the new EFI is located on the hard disk. In theory, this makes the whole system more flexible, with more space for fancy screens and wizards for the setup settings. In practice, it's a shit system which makes installing, cloning and backup a pain in the ass.

GPT is the disk partitioning scheme that goes together with EFI. The fancy screens and wizards scripts are located on a separate partition called /efi, and the computer knows to look for this partition first to load the 'bios' settings. The alternative, without /efi partition and regular BIOS, is called MBR.

If the /efi partition is not there, but the computer expects it, you will get the errors like you get. In your other comment, there is no mention of an /efi partition.

What is successful for me every time though, is creating a live USB flash drive with the desired OS, booting from this USB into the OS, and then choosing Full Install to the hard disk. This will take care of the UEFI/GPT crap automagically. I have installed Linux Mint 17.2 and 17.3 Cinnamon on physical and virtual machines this way without a hiccup.

If you dare, you could try to wipe the entire hard drive. Not just the partitions, but the whole disk, including the boot sector and partition table. This is potentially catastrophical if you choose the wrong disk, so double check.

Boot to a live linux os. CD, DVD, flash drive, whatever.

Identify the target disk with GParted (/dev/sda, /dev/sdb, ...)

Open a terminal and do

sudo dd /dev/zero <insert target drive here> bs=1M

this will duplicate (dd) the disk '/dev/zero', which is essentially a fake disk with all zeroes, to your target drive, with a block size of 1M. The process will seem to hang, but exit to prompt when the end of the target disk is reached. Make sure you don't speficy a partition for the target drive (e.g. /dev/sdc2) but the target drive itself (/dev/sdc).

Now you should have a factory-clean disk without MBR, GPT or other information. Install linux from the live usb stick and it should take care of the mbr/efi stuff by itself.

Good luck man.

As for your question: I have had some success with Boot-Repair. It's for Ubuntu but works lovely on Mint. Get it with

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:yannubuntu/boot-repair
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install boot-repair

Caution: don't use the automatic function, but click on 'Advanced Options'. This will let you specify exactly what you want to do in several tabs. Only thing is that it will add every bootable partition on each and every attached disk to Grub, so you might want to disconnect/disable some drives before you do this.
